title: How would you estimate how many ride-hailing trips are taken in London each day?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many ride-hailing trips are taken in London each day?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: London sees roughly 450,000 ride-hailing trips a day: about 405,000 by residents (3% of 9M people riding, at 1.5 trips each) and about 45,000 by commuters and visitors. Because only a small share of people ride on any given day, that share drives the whole answer, so build it carefully and check it against the number of drivers. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many ride-hailing trips are taken in London each day?

Define three things up front:

  • What counts: app-booked private hire trips (Uber, Bolt and similar). Black cabs hailed on the street are out; minicabs booked by phone are a grey area, so say what you choose.
  • Where: trips that start within Greater London, whoever takes them. That includes visitors and commuters, and trips that start at Heathrow.
  • When: an average day across the year, not a Friday night.
"I'll estimate app-booked private hire trips starting in Greater London on an average day, including trips by visitors and commuters."

The approach: people × share riding today × trips each

Ride-hailing is a daily-flow question, so think about a single day: people in London × share who take a ride today × trips per rider. Split residents from non-residents, because visitors and commuters behave differently from locals and are easy to forget.

A small share drives everything here: 3% versus 4% changes the answer by a third. So build it from behaviour you can picture rather than plucking it from the air.

Step by step

1. Residents

  1. People in London: 9M (the ONS estimate for mid-2024 is about 9.1M).
  2. Share taking a trip today: 3%. Picture it: perhaps a third of Londoners use ride-hailing at all, and a typical user rides about once every ten days, so about 3% ride on any given day.
  3. Trips per rider: 1.5. Some ride one way and take the Tube back; some ride both ways.
  4. 9M × 3% × 1.5 = 405,000 trips.

2. Commuters and visitors

  1. Assume 1.5M non-residents in London on an average day: commuters from outside, tourists and business visitors.
  2. 2% take a ride × 1.5 trips = 45,000 trips. Visitors ride more than residents, but most commuters take the train in and out, so 2% overall is a fair blend.

3. Total

405,000 + 45,000 = about 450,000 trips a day, or roughly 165M a year.

Sanity check from the supply side

Transport for London licensed about 110,000 private hire drivers in mid-2026. Not all of them drive on a given day, and the licence covers traditional minicab and chauffeur work as well as app-based driving. Assume half are working on an average day: about 55,000 drivers. If each completes 8 trips, that is 440,000 trips, within a few per cent of the demand-side 450,000.

Both routes rely on assumptions, but they are independent assumptions. When demand and supply land close together, you can be more confident in the answer. If supply had come out at 2 million, you would revisit the 3% first.

Which assumption matters most?

The daily riding share among residents. At 2% instead of 3%, resident trips fall to 270,000 and the total to about 315,000. Trips per rider and the visitor numbers matter much less.

What a strong answer sounds like

"About 450,000 trips a day. Most come from residents: 3% of 9 million riding on a given day, about 1.5 trips each, which I get from a third of Londoners using the apps roughly every ten days. Visitors and commuters add about 45,000. On the supply side, about 55,000 active drivers doing 8 trips each gives 440,000, so the two views agree. The number to test is that 3%."

A weak answer says "maybe 10% of Londoners take an Uber every day, so 900,000", which would need roughly twice the active drivers the supply side can support, and never checks.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting non-residents. Visitors and commuters are a real slice of trips, especially from airports and stations.
  • Confusing riders and trips. One rider often makes two trips.
  • Using the average for capacity. Friday nights, bad weather, Tube strikes and airport peaks push demand far above the average. A platform case cares about those hours.
  • Mixing requested and completed trips. Cancellations and unmet requests mean demand is higher than completed trips at peak times.

Practise it

1. The average fare is $20 and the platform keeps 25%. What is the platforms' combined daily and yearly revenue?

Show the answer

Gross bookings: 450,000 × $20 = $9M a day. Platform share: 25% = $2.25M a day, or about $820M a year (× 365).

2. If each active driver could complete 10 trips a day, how many active drivers would 450,000 trips need?

Show the answer

450,000 ÷ 10 = 45,000 drivers. Better matching (less waiting between trips) means fewer drivers for the same demand, or more trips per driver and higher earnings.

3. On a rainy Friday, the resident riding share doubles to 6% and everything else is unchanged. How many trips?

Show the answer

Residents: 9M × 6% × 1.5 = 810,000. Add 45,000 for visitors: 855,000 trips, nearly double an average day. With about 55,000 drivers at 8 trips (440,000), the platforms could not meet that, which is why prices surge.

Where to practise next

Ride-hailing is a two-sided market; read what network effects are and how to handle a platform case, then try the RideNow drivers case. For another daily-flow estimate, see Heathrow passengers, and practise more in the market sizing drills.
